config.title: Lippincott Micro/Immuno Block 1 QBank
config.subtitle: Selected questions from Chapters 2 (Virology), 6 (Basic Immunology), and 7 (Clinical Immunology)

questions.stem: A new antiviral agent is found to prevent uncoating in a number of different viruses. At which part in the generalized virus replication cycle does uncoating occur?
choices: Attachment, Penetration, Replication, Assembly, Release, Uncoating
Attachment, Penetration, Replication, Assembly, Uncoating, Release
Attachment, Penetration, Uncoating, Replication, Assembly, Release
Attachment, Uncoating, Penetration, Assembly, Replication, Release
Uncoating, Attachment, Penetration, Replication, Assembly, Release
questions.explanation: The generalized virus replication cycle proceeds in order: attachment of the virus to a host cell receptor, penetration into the cell, uncoating of the genome from its protein capsid, replication of the genome, assembly of new virions, and release from the cell. Uncoating must occur after penetration and before replication because the polymerase machinery needs access to the naked genome. Any answer sequence placing uncoating before penetration or after replication misorders the cycle.
keypoints: ⭐ Standard order: Attachment → Penetration → Uncoating → Replication → Assembly → Release
Uncoating releases the viral genome from the capsid so it is accessible to polymerases
Enveloped viruses often uncoat via fusion of the envelope with host membranes during penetration
Antivirals like amantadine target the uncoating step of influenza A by blocking the M2 ion channel

questions.stem: A new immune modulator is developed which enhances early immunologic responses to viral infection. Which of the following is the earliest immunological event that could be the target of this new drug?
choices: Activation of naïve viral-specific B cells
Activation of naïve viral-specific T cells
Production of IFN-γ by antiviral cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Natural killer (NK) cells are part of the innate immune response and are among the earliest defenses mounted against viral infection, acting within hours. Virally infected cells commonly downregulate MHC class I expression, and NK cells recognize and kill these MHC-deficient cells without requiring prior antigen-specific priming. The remaining options are all components of the adaptive immune response, which requires dendritic cell antigen presentation in lymph nodes and takes days to become active.
keypoints: ⭐ NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virally infected cells lacking MHC class I ('missing self' recognition)
Adaptive responses (T and B cell activation) require dendritic cell antigen presentation in draining lymph nodes and take days
Dendritic cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity by maturing and presenting antigen to naive T cells
Type I interferons are also part of the early innate antiviral response, inducing an antiviral state in neighboring cells

questions.stem: Amantadine is a drug used to reduce the ill effects of an influenza virus A infection; however, increasing levels of resistance have limited its usefulness. Resistant strains of influenza A contain single amino acid substitutions in the M2 protein. With which aspect of the virus replication cycle is this protein involved?
questions.explanation: The influenza A M2 protein is an ion channel that translocates hydrogen ions from the endosome into the interior of the virion after endocytosis, lowering the internal pH. This acidification triggers fusion of the viral envelope with the endosomal membrane and release of the viral RNA from the capsid, a process called uncoating. Amantadine and rimantadine block the M2 ion channel, preventing uncoating; resistance arises from point mutations in the M2 transmembrane domain.
keypoints: ⭐ M2 protein = proton channel that acidifies the virion interior, triggering uncoating
Amantadine/rimantadine block M2 and are only active against influenza A (not B, which lacks M2)
Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir) act at a different step — viral release — and work against both influenza A and B
M2 channel-blocker resistance is now widespread, limiting amantadine's clinical usefulness

questions.stem: HIV can infect any cell expressing the appropriate coreceptors but a productive infection occurs only in activated cells. What is the most likely reason for this observation?
choices: Activated cells decrease their cell surface expression of the coreceptors, so budding virions can easily escape to infect new host cells
Activated cells do not have the capacity to induce the antiviral state
Resting cells have sensitive TLR molecules which bind HIV RNA molecules and activate the antiviral state, resulting in degradation of the integrated HIV DNA
Activated cells express transcription factors and polymerases required for transcription of HIV genes
Resting cells are resistant to HIV attachment and penetration due to low expression of the HIV coreceptors
questions.explanation: HIV requires host-cell transcription factors (such as NF-κB) and active RNA polymerase II machinery to transcribe its integrated proviral DNA into viral mRNA. Resting T cells lack sufficient levels of these activated transcription factors, so although HIV can attach and even integrate into resting cells, productive viral gene expression and replication only proceed once the cell becomes activated. This is why HIV establishes latent reservoirs in resting memory CD4+ T cells.
keypoints: ⭐ HIV transcription depends on host activation-induced transcription factors (e.g., NF-κB), not on cell surface receptor levels
Activated CD4+ T cells actually increase surface CD4, CCR5, and CXCR4 expression, not decrease it
This dependency on cellular activation is the basis for latent HIV reservoirs in resting memory T cells, a major barrier to cure
HIV Nef and Vpr proteins manipulate the host cell cycle and immune evasion but are distinct from the transcription-activation requirement

questions.stem: In January, a 66-year-old woman presents with a fever of 102°F, chills, back pain, headache, and marked fatigue. Her physician prescribes oseltamivir and she rapidly recovers. With which etiologic agent was she infected?
questions.explanation: The winter timing (January), abrupt onset of high fever, chills, myalgia/back pain, headache, and profound fatigue is the classic presentation of influenza. Oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor, is specifically indicated for treatment of influenza A and B and shortens illness duration when given early. The other listed pathogens do not typically respond to oseltamivir and have different clinical patterns (e.g., RSV causes bronchiolitis in infants, parainfluenza causes croup).
keypoints: ⭐ Classic flu triad: abrupt fever, myalgia, and profound fatigue, peaking in winter months
Oseltamivir and zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors effective against both influenza A and B
Amantadine/rimantadine only work against influenza A and are limited by widespread M2 resistance
Early initiation (within 48 hours of symptom onset) of oseltamivir is needed for maximal benefit

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir?
choices: Directly prevents replication of the viral genome
Prevents the release of mature virions from the infected host cell
Inhibits the uncoating of the virus
Inhibits the translocation of the viral genome to the nucleus
Binds directly to the virus RNA polymerase active site
questions.explanation: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is a neuraminidase inhibitor. Neuraminidase normally cleaves sialic acid residues on the host cell surface, which is necessary to release newly budded influenza virions that would otherwise remain bound via viral hemagglutinin. By inhibiting neuraminidase, oseltamivir traps progeny virions on the surface of the infected cell, preventing their release and spread to new cells. It does not act on genome replication, uncoating, or nuclear transport.
keypoints: ⭐ Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release budding virions; inhibiting it traps virus at the cell surface
Sialic acid also serves as the influenza attachment receptor, so neuraminidase functions in both entry and egress
Zanamivir shares this same mechanism and is also active against influenza A and B
Contrast with amantadine, which blocks the M2 channel and thus blocks uncoating instead of release

questions.stem: Type I interferon is used in the treatment of certain viral infections. Which one of the following best describes the mode of action of this antiviral?
choices: Decreases class I MHC expression of infected host cells
Increases degradation of mRNA of infected host cells
Decreases expression of viral receptors on the surface of host cells
Directly lyses free virions in the blood
Attaches to free virus and provides a binding site for opsonizing antibodies
questions.explanation: Type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β) are secreted by virally infected cells and act on neighboring uninfected cells to induce an 'antiviral state.' This state involves activation of pathways (e.g., 2'-5' oligoadenylate synthetase/RNase L and PKR) that inhibit protein synthesis and degrade both host and viral mRNA, limiting viral replication. Contrary to intuition, type I interferons actually upregulate (not decrease) MHC class I expression, enhancing recognition of infected cells by cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
keypoints: ⭐ Type I IFN induces mRNA degradation and translational shutdown in neighboring cells via RNase L and PKR pathways
Type I IFN upregulates MHC class I expression, improving CD8+ T cell recognition of infected cells
Used clinically for chronic hepatitis B/C and some HPV-related conditions
Distinct from type II interferon (IFN-γ), which is produced by activated T cells and NK cells and primarily activates macrophages

questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis B is treated with a regimen that included pegylated interferon-α. Shortly after initiating therapy, the patient's serum liver enzymes increase, indicating liver cell death. What mechanism of action of α-interferon could account for this transient spike in serum liver enzymes?
choices: Down-regulation of expression of viral proteins on infected cells
Increased expression of MHC-I on infected cells
Interference with DNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity
questions.explanation: Interferon-α upregulates MHC class I gene expression on infected hepatocytes, enhancing their recognition and killing by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. This increased immune-mediated clearance of infected hepatocytes produces a transient rise in liver enzymes (ALT/AST) early in therapy, reflecting increased hepatocyte destruction rather than direct drug hepatotoxicity. This is a distinct mechanism from the direct antiviral effects of nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors used in HBV.
keypoints: ⭐ IFN-α upregulates MHC-I, boosting CTL-mediated killing of infected hepatocytes — this explains the enzyme flare
This flare is generally considered a sign of effective immune-mediated viral clearance, not drug toxicity
IFN-α has multiple additional poorly characterized antiviral gene induction effects beyond MHC upregulation
Contrast with lamivudine, which directly inhibits HBV reverse transcriptase rather than acting immunologically

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man was clinically diagnosed with the flu after presenting with a fever of 102°F, severe myalgia, fatigue, and rhinorrhea of 12 h duration. The physician had read local health department reports that said both AH1N1 and B viruses were circulating in the area. Which medication did the physician most likely prescribe?
questions.explanation: Because both influenza A (H1N1) and influenza B strains were circulating, the physician needed an agent effective against both types. Zanamivir and oseltamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors active against both influenza A and B, whereas amantadine and rimantadine (M2 channel blockers) work only against influenza A. Foscarnet is used for CMV/resistant herpesvirus infections, ribavirin for hepatitis C or RSV, and ritonavir is an HIV protease inhibitor — none are appropriate here.
keypoints: ⭐ Neuraminidase inhibitors (zanamivir, oseltamivir) cover both influenza A and B; M2 blockers (amantadine, rimantadine) cover only influenza A
Influenza B lacks the M2 ion channel, explaining amantadine's lack of activity against it
Early treatment (within 48 hours of onset) with neuraminidase inhibitors reduces illness duration
Local surveillance data on circulating strains should guide empiric antiviral selection during flu season

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl was brought to the emergency department with a 3-day history of a coldlike illness and a 1-day history of difficulty breathing and an unusual, barklike cough. Physical exam revealed fever, tachypnea, tachycardia, and stridor. A chest radiograph revealed narrowing of the upper airways (a steeple sign), with lungs free of infiltrates. A rapid antigen detection test was positive for parainfluenza virus. What is the clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The barklike cough, stridor, and radiographic 'steeple sign' (subglottic narrowing) in a young child are classic for croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus types 1–3. The absence of infiltrates on chest radiograph argues against pneumonia and bronchiolitis, and the clinical picture and age are not typical for bacterial epiglottitis, which presents with a toxic-appearing child, drooling, and a thumbprint sign rather than a steeple sign.
keypoints: ⭐ Steeple sign on neck/chest X-ray + barky cough + stridor = croup, classically due to parainfluenza virus
Croup most commonly affects children under 3 years old
Epiglottitis (thumbprint sign, drooling, toxic appearance) is a key mimicker to distinguish, historically caused by H. influenzae type b
Bronchiolitis (wheezing, infants <2 years) is most often caused by RSV rather than parainfluenza

questions.stem: A 21-year-old college student contracted mumps infection as did several other students at the college. He had received a single dose of the MMR vaccine at 15 months of age. What is the most likely reason that he became infected despite having been vaccinated?
choices: Early vaccines only contained one of the four strains of mumps virus
Early versions of the mumps vaccine were heat inactivated and induced immune suppression in some recipients
Fifteen months of age is too early to receive the MMR vaccine
Mumps virus rapidly undergoes antigenic variation
Some individuals who receive a single dose of mumps vaccine do not respond adequately
questions.explanation: A single dose of live attenuated MMR vaccine is only about 90% effective, meaning a meaningful minority of vaccinated individuals remain susceptible to mumps, measles, or rubella. Mumps virus exists as a single serotype and does not undergo rapid antigenic variation, ruling out that explanation. This incomplete single-dose efficacy is why a second MMR dose (recommended since 1989, originally to address measles outbreaks in vaccinated populations) is now part of the standard schedule, improving population immunity, particularly relevant in crowded settings like college campuses.
keypoints: ⭐ Single-dose MMR efficacy is ~90%, leaving a subset of vaccinees susceptible — hence the two-dose schedule
Mumps virus has only one serotype, unlike influenza, so antigenic drift/shift is not the explanation
College campuses/dormitories are classic settings for mumps outbreaks due to close contact among partially immune populations
The second MMR dose was added to the schedule in 1989 following vaccinated-population measles outbreaks

questions.stem: Five patients aged 45 to 67 were admitted to an urban hospital between February and March with severe pneumonia. Clinical manifestations included high fever, nonproductive cough, and dense lower lobe infiltrates. All had underlying lung disease or were smokers. Gram stain of sputum showed no pathogens, and patients did not respond to empiric antibiotics; bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. A DNA virus was isolated in cell culture. Which virus is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus is a DNA virus that can cause severe pneumonia, particularly in adults with underlying lung disease, smokers, or immunocompromised patients, and it will not respond to antibacterial therapy or grow on standard bacterial/fungal cultures. The other listed viruses (hantavirus, influenza, parainfluenza, RSV) are all RNA viruses, which excludes them given the question specifies a DNA virus was isolated.
keypoints: ⭐ Adenovirus is the DNA virus among common respiratory pathogens — key distinguishing fact for this question type
Adenovirus causes a spectrum of illness: conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, and pneumonia, especially in outbreaks (military recruits, camps)
Failure to respond to empiric antibiotics with negative bacterial/fungal cultures should prompt consideration of viral pneumonia
Underlying lung disease and smoking are risk factors for more severe adenoviral respiratory infection in adults

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with a 3-day history of cough, a profusely runny nose, and conjunctivitis, and a 1-day history of 40°C fever and a blotchy, erythematous, maculopapular rash that began on his face and is now appearing on his chest. The child is toxic appearing. His history is significant for a lack of most childhood vaccines due to family religious beliefs. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The prodrome of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis ('the three C's') followed by a high fever and a cephalocaudally spreading blotchy maculopapular rash is classic for measles (rubeola). The lack of vaccination is a critical risk factor given how effective MMR vaccination is at preventing measles. Mumps presents primarily with parotitis, rubella is typically a mild illness with low-grade fever, and varicella produces an itchy vesicular (not maculopapular) rash with lesions in different stages.
keypoints: ⭐ Measles prodrome: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (the '3 C's') followed by cephalocaudal maculopapular rash
Koplik spots (bluish-white spots on buccal mucosa) are a pathognomonic early finding not mentioned here but classically precede the rash
Unvaccinated status is the key epidemiologic clue pointing away from a vaccine-preventable illness rarity
Measles can cause serious complications including pneumonia, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)

questions.stem: A child with measles recovered uneventfully, was re-exposed to the same agent a year later, but did not become ill. What prevented the child from becoming infected on subsequent encounter with the agent?
choices: Naïve cytotoxic T cells specific for the agent
Neutralizing IgG antibodies specific for the agent
questions.explanation: Although innate defenses (NK cells, interferon, macrophages) and cell-mediated immunity contribute to initial recovery from viral infection, long-term protection against reinfection is primarily mediated by pathogen-specific neutralizing IgG antibodies generated during the adaptive humoral response. These antibodies persist after infection (or vaccination) and can block the virus from infecting cells upon re-exposure, providing durable immunity. The T cells involved in a memory response would be memory, not naïve, cytotoxic T cells.
keypoints: ⭐ Durable protection against reinfection is primarily due to pathogen-specific neutralizing IgG antibodies from the humoral response
Innate defenses (NK cells, macrophages, type I IFN) act early but do not confer lasting specific immunity
Memory (not naïve) T and B cells mediate anamnestic responses on re-exposure — the answer choice specifying 'naïve' cytotoxic T cells is therefore wrong
This principle underlies the effectiveness of live attenuated vaccines like MMR in inducing durable humoral immunity

questions.stem: A 9-month-old child is hospitalized with viral pneumonia. Which virus is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is by far the most common cause of viral pneumonia and bronchiolitis in infants under 1 year of age. While adenovirus, influenza, and parainfluenza can all cause pneumonia in children, RSV predominates in this specific young age group, especially during its seasonal peak (fall to spring). Palivizumab, a monoclonal antibody against the RSV fusion protein, is used prophylactically in high-risk premature infants.
keypoints: ⭐ RSV is the leading cause of viral pneumonia/bronchiolitis in infants under 1 year of age
Palivizumab (anti-fusion protein monoclonal antibody) is given prophylactically to high-risk premature infants during RSV season
RSV lacks a hemagglutinin-neuraminidase protein, unlike the closely related parainfluenza viruses
Parainfluenza virus is the classic cause of croup, a distinct clinical entity from RSV bronchiolitis/pneumonia

questions.stem: A 4-month-old child develops a viral infection with fever and vesicular lesions in the anterior portion of the mouth, as well as around the mouth. This infection occurred 2 weeks after her mother had a cold sore. The lesions lasted for about 3 weeks during which time the child was not eating or drinking normally. Which of the following will be the most likely consequence of this infection in the child?
questions.explanation: This case describes primary herpetic gingivostomatitis due to herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), transmitted from the mother's cold sore. After primary infection, HSV-1 establishes lifelong latency in sensory (trigeminal) ganglia, with periodic reactivation causing recurrent cold sores or asymptomatic shedding. Complete clearance of the virus from the body does not occur with herpesviruses. Encephalitis, esophagitis, and keratitis are possible but rarer complications, generally seen in immunocompromised hosts rather than being the expected typical outcome.
keypoints: ⭐ HSV-1 establishes lifelong latency in the trigeminal ganglia after primary gingivostomatitis, with periodic reactivation
Primary infection typically occurs via contact with someone shedding virus (symptomatic or asymptomatic)
Complete viral clearance does not occur with herpesviruses — this is a key distinguishing concept from many other viral infections
Antiviral cell-mediated immunity (T cell-mediated, IFN-γ) is thought to be key to maintaining latency and limiting recurrences

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy attending a 4-week summer camp presented in August with a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, and conjunctivitis with a gritty feeling in the eyes. Seven other children and two camp counselors developed similar symptoms over the next few days. A similar outbreak occurred at the camp in July. The outbreak was traced to the camp's underchlorinated, turbid swimming pool. Which virus is the cause of this outbreak?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus is the most common cause of outbreaks of pharyngoconjunctival fever, particularly associated with poorly chlorinated, turbid swimming pools in camps and community settings. Adenovirus is a nonenveloped DNA virus that is relatively resistant to environmental degradation and disinfection, allowing it to persist and spread via water exposure. The other viruses listed are not classically associated with swimming pool-related outbreaks of fever, sore throat, and conjunctivitis.
keypoints: ⭐ Adenovirus causes pharyngoconjunctival fever, classically linked to inadequately chlorinated swimming pools ('pool conjunctivitis')
As a nonenveloped virus, adenovirus is relatively resistant to environmental conditions and disinfectants, aiding waterborne transmission
Outbreak settings like camps, schools, and military barracks are classic epidemiologic clues for adenovirus
Adenovirus can also cause epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, a more severe ocular presentation

questions.stem: An individual is infected with a virus that replicates causing clinical manifestations. The manifestations later subside; however, virus is not cleared from the body. Viral replication occurs continuously throughout life. Which term describes this type of infection?
questions.explanation: This describes a chronic persistent viral infection, in which the virus is never cleared and continues to replicate continuously (as opposed to intermittently) throughout the host's life, as seen with infections like chronic hepatitis B or C. This differs from latent infection, in which there is only intermittent (not continuous) viral replication with periods of quiescence, and from slow viral infections, in which manifestations of disease are delayed for years to decades after initial infection (e.g., prion diseases, though these are not technically viral).
keypoints: ⭐ Chronic infection = continuous ongoing viral replication without clearance (e.g., chronic HBV/HCV)
Latent infection = intermittent replication with quiescent periods punctuated by reactivation (e.g., HSV, VZV)
Slow infection = long delay (years-decades) before disease manifestations appear, classically associated with prion diseases
Acute infection results in either complete clearance or death of the host, unlike persistent infections

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman refuses to be vaccinated against influenza virus because she was vaccinated the previous year. What changes in the virus necessitate annual vaccination?
choices: Acquisition of new genes through coinfection of cells with parainfluenza viruses
Antigenic changes in the viral matrix protein
Changes in the level of expression of the envelope fusion proteins
Mutations in the genes for the envelope glycoproteins
Reassortment of RNA strands between animal and human strains
questions.explanation: Influenza viruses undergo frequent point mutations in the genes encoding the envelope glycoproteins hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), a process called antigenic drift. This year-to-year antigenic drift is why new vaccines must be formulated annually to match the predominant circulating serotypes. Antigenic shift — reassortment of RNA segments between different influenza A strains infecting the same host — is a much rarer event responsible for pandemics, but is not the reason for routine annual vaccination.
keypoints: ⭐ Antigenic drift = gradual point mutations in HA/NA genes, necessitating yearly vaccine reformulation
Antigenic shift = reassortment of RNA segments between influenza A strains (e.g., human and animal strains), causing rare pandemics
Influenza A has 8 separate RNA segments, enabling reassortment when a cell is co-infected with two different strains
Influenza B is not divided into subtypes like A and undergoes only antigenic drift, being more genetically stable

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman is hospitalized with a fever of unknown origin. An elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) suggest an ongoing systemic inflammatory response. Which cytokine is especially important in inducing elevations in CRP and ESR?
questions.explanation: IL-6, released from activated macrophages and other cells during systemic inflammation, is the primary cytokine driving hepatocytes to produce acute phase reactants such as CRP and fibrinogen. Elevated fibrinogen increases red cell rouleaux formation, which raises the ESR, while CRP itself functions as an opsonin. Although IL-1 and TNF-α also contribute to the acute phase response, IL-6 is the dominant inducer of hepatic acute phase protein synthesis.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-6 is the principal cytokine driving hepatic acute phase protein synthesis (CRP, fibrinogen)
ESR reflects fibrinogen-driven red cell rouleaux formation, not CRP directly
IL-1 and TNF-α also contribute to acute phase responses but are secondary to IL-6 in this role
CRP acts as an opsonin, enhancing phagocytosis of pathogens coated with it

questions.stem: A 10-month-old male with a history of recurrent, serious extracellular bacterial infections is hospitalized with pneumonia due to Pneumocystis jeroveci. An immunologic workup reveals neutropenia, normal numbers of T and B cells, normal complement levels and activity, elevated IgM, and very low IgG and IgA. What immunologic function is impaired in this child that best explains the infection?
choices: B-cell migration to follicles in secondary lymphoid tissue
Differentiation of B and T cells from precursor cells
Expression of functional antigen receptors on T cells
T-cell activation of macrophages and class switching in B cells
questions.explanation: This case describes hyper-IgM syndrome, caused by deficient expression of CD40 ligand (CD154) on activated T cells. The interaction of CD40L with CD40 on B cells is required both for immunoglobulin class switching (explaining the elevated IgM with low IgG/IgA) and for T-cell-mediated activation of macrophages (explaining susceptibility to Pneumocystis jeroveci, an intracellular-type pathogen requiring cell-mediated defenses). T- and B-cell numbers remain normal because lymphocyte development itself is intact; only these downstream CD40L-dependent functions are impaired.
keypoints: ⭐ Hyper-IgM syndrome = CD40L (CD154) deficiency on T cells, impairing both B-cell class switching and macrophage activation
Elevated IgM with low IgG/IgA is the classic lab signature of hyper-IgM syndrome
Susceptibility to Pneumocystis jeroveci reflects the T-cell/macrophage activation defect, not humoral immunity alone
X-linked inheritance pattern (affected males) is typical, as CD40L is encoded on the X chromosome

questions.stem: A 6-month-old male is hospitalized with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex. His history is significant for recurrent episodes of otitis media which responded poorly to antibiotics and episodes of severe thrush and diaper rash. Based on this history, an immunologic workup was done and the child was diagnosed with an immune deficiency disorder. Deficiencies of which aspect of the immune response could best account for this child's medical history?
questions.explanation: This child's infections span both intracellular pathogens (disseminated M. avium, controlled by cell-mediated/T-cell immunity) and extracellular pathogens plus Candida (otitis media from encapsulated bacteria, controlled by humoral immunity, and mucocutaneous candidiasis, which requires T-cell-mediated activation of phagocytes). This combined pattern of susceptibility to both intracellular and extracellular organisms, plus fungal infection, points to a combined B- and T-cell defect rather than an isolated deficiency in any single arm.
keypoints: ⭐ Intracellular pathogen control (e.g., mycobacteria) depends on cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity; extracellular pathogen control depends on humoral (B-cell/antibody) immunity
Combined B- and T-cell defects (as in SCID) produce susceptibility to both types of pathogens plus opportunistic fungal infection
Candida albicans overgrowth (thrush, diaper rash) occurs when T cells cannot activate phagocytic macrophages
This presentation pattern helps localize an immunodeficiency to a specific arm of the immune system on exams

questions.stem: A 14-year-old male child with extensive third-degree burns from a house fire receives a skin graft. Skin grafted from which donor has the lowest risk of immunologic rejection?
questions.explanation: An autograft — tissue transplanted from one site to another within the same individual — carries essentially no risk of immunologic rejection because the donor and recipient are genetically identical (self tissue). Grafts from a fraternal (dizygotic) twin, a parent, or any other relative are allografts, since fraternal twins are genetically distinct individuals (unlike identical/monozygotic twins) and therefore express different MHC molecules that can trigger an immune rejection response.
keypoints: ⭐ Autografts (self-to-self) have essentially zero immunologic rejection risk since there is no MHC mismatch
Fraternal (dizygotic) twins are genetically distinct, unlike identical (monozygotic) twins, and are treated immunologically as allografts
Autograft failure can still occur mechanically (e.g., poor vascularization) but not via immune rejection
Isografts (between identical twins) would be the next lowest-risk category after autografts

questions.stem: A 36-year-old female is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. What were her most likely clinical manifestations?
choices: Abdominal pain, weight loss, and bloody diarrhea
Drooping of her eyelids and muscle weakness that improves with rest
Goiter, palpitations, and proptosis of the eyes
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis classically presents with fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with sustained activity and improves with rest, frequently first affecting extraocular and eyelid muscles, producing ptosis (drooping eyelids) and diplopia. This pattern reflects progressive depletion of functional acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction with repeated use. The other options describe distinct conditions: inflammatory bowel disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, hemolytic anemia, and Graves disease, respectively.
keypoints: ⭐ Hallmark of myasthenia gravis: fatigable muscle weakness, worse with activity, improved with rest; ptosis/diplopia are classic early signs
Symptoms fluctuate through the day, often worsening toward evening
Thymic abnormalities (hyperplasia or thymoma) are commonly associated and thymectomy can improve symptoms
Diagnosis can be supported by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody testing or edrophonium (Tensilon) test

questions.stem: What is the immunopathogenesis of myasthenia gravis (in the patient from the previous question)?
choices: Antibody-mediated hemolysis of red blood cells
Antibody-mediated stimulation of the thyroid gland
Immunologic attack of peripheral nerve myelin sheath
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is a type II hypersensitivity (antibody-mediated) autoimmune disease in which autoantibodies bind to and block or downregulate acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction. This prevents effective depolarization of the muscle membrane despite normal acetylcholine release and degradation, so muscle activity progressively weakens with repeated use as available functional receptors are further reduced by receptor internalization/complement-mediated destruction.
keypoints: ⭐ Myasthenia gravis is a type II hypersensitivity reaction: autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction
Contrast with Graves disease, where stimulating (not blocking) autoantibodies target the TSH receptor
Contrast with Guillain-Barré syndrome, which involves autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin
Plasmapheresis and IVIG can be used for acute myasthenic crises by removing or neutralizing pathogenic autoantibodies

questions.stem: The repression of which transcription factor explains on a molecular level the anti-inflammatory effect of corticosteroids?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids exert their anti-inflammatory effects largely by inhibiting the transcription factor NF-κB (along with AP-1 and NFAT), which normally drives transcription of genes encoding proinflammatory cytokines and proteins needed for immune cell activation and proliferation. By repressing NF-κB activity, corticosteroids broadly reduce the transcription of inflammatory mediators. FoxP3 is a transcription factor specific to regulatory T cells and is not the mechanism of corticosteroid action; the other listed molecules are components of signal transduction rather than transcription factors.
keypoints: ⭐ Corticosteroids act in large part by repressing NF-κB, blocking transcription of proinflammatory cytokine genes
AP-1 and NFAT are additional transcription factors also inhibited by corticosteroids
FoxP3 is the master transcription factor for regulatory T cell development/function, unrelated to corticosteroid mechanism
This broad transcriptional repression explains the wide-ranging immunosuppressive effects of corticosteroids across cell types

questions.stem: Which of the following cytokines supports proliferation and differentiation of developing lymphocytes in the primary lymphoid tissue?
questions.explanation: IL-7 is essential for proliferation and differentiation of developing lymphocytes within primary lymphoid tissue (bone marrow and thymus). IL-1 is an inflammatory cytokine produced by phagocytes rather than a lymphopoietic factor. IL-4 promotes differentiation of mature Th2 CD4+ T cells in the periphery, while IL-12 and IL-18 drive Th1 differentiation — none of these act on developing lymphocytes in primary lymphoid organs.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-7 is the key cytokine for lymphocyte development in primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow, thymus)
Defects in IL-7 receptor signaling (e.g., common gamma chain mutations) cause forms of SCID
IL-12 and IL-18 act later, in the periphery, to promote Th1 differentiation of mature CD4+ T cells
Contrast primary lymphoid tissue (site of lymphocyte development) with secondary lymphoid tissue (site of immune response, e.g., lymph nodes, spleen)

questions.stem: A workup on an ill child revealed low levels of complement C3 in her blood. Which one of the following presentations did this child most likely manifest?
questions.explanation: C3 is central to all three complement activation pathways; its cleavage to C3b enables opsonization of pathogens, while C3a/C5a recruit phagocytes and the downstream membrane attack complex lyses target cells. C3 deficiency therefore severely impairs innate defense against extracellular bacteria, leading to recurrent pyogenic infections, particularly with encapsulated organisms. The other listed conditions (eczema, hemolytic anemia, viral infection recovery, vaccine response) are not primarily complement-dependent processes.
keypoints: ⭐ C3 is the convergence point of all three complement pathways (classical, alternative, lectin) — its deficiency impairs opsonization broadly
C3b acts as the major opsonin, enhancing phagocytosis by complement receptor-bearing phagocytes
Terminal complement (C5-C9/MAC) deficiencies classically predispose to Neisseria infections specifically, distinct from early complement (C3) deficiency
C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that recruit and activate phagocytes to the infection site

questions.stem: Vaccination operates to generate a humoral immune response to the immunogen(s). Which one of the following represents the critical function of the resultant humoral response in protecting vaccinated patients from future infections by targeted pathogenic agents?
questions.explanation: While vaccine-induced antibodies can mediate opsonization, complement activation, and ADCC, the most critical protective function is neutralization — blocking the pathogen from attaching to and infecting host cells in the first place. This preemptive blockade prevents colonization entirely, offering the most complete protection, whereas the other mechanisms only act after the pathogen has already begun to establish infection in tissue.
keypoints: ⭐ Neutralization prevents pathogen attachment/entry into host cells, stopping infection before it starts — the ideal vaccine-mediated defense
Extravasation refers to immune cell migration from blood into tissue, not an antibody function
Opsonization, complement activation, and ADCC all act on pathogens that have already colonized or infected tissue
IgG is the antibody class most associated with these memory-response protective functions after vaccination

questions.stem: Positive selection in the thymus occurs when thymocytes express functional versions of which critical molecule?
questions.explanation: Double-positive (CD4+CD8+) thymocytes interact with MHC class I and II expressed on thymic epithelial cells; those that express a functional T-cell receptor capable of recognizing self-MHC survive this positive selection step and progress to single-positive (CD4 or CD8) status. CD28 mediates costimulation but is not the molecule being tested in positive selection, and while thymocytes do express MHC class I and Fc receptors, these are not the determinants of positive selection survival.
keypoints: ⭐ Positive selection tests for a functional TCR capable of binding self-MHC with low-to-moderate affinity
Thymocytes that fail positive selection (non-functional TCR/no self-MHC binding) die by neglect
Following positive selection, double-positive thymocytes become single-positive (CD4+ or CD8+) based on which MHC class they recognized
Negative selection (a separate later step) removes thymocytes with TCRs that bind self-antigen too strongly

questions.stem: Which one of the following represents the major role of negative selection in the thymus?
choices: Maturation of professional antigen presenting cells such as dendritic cells
Expression of T-cell receptors on mature T cells
Differentiation of Th1 and Th2 CD4+ T cells
questions.explanation: Negative selection eliminates T cells whose TCRs bind self-antigens presented on MHC with excessive affinity, inducing apoptosis in these self-reactive clones. Thymic medullary epithelial cells express the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene, which drives ectopic expression of a broad range of tissue-specific self-antigens for this purpose. Approximately 90% of thymocytes are eliminated during selection processes, underscoring how central this tolerance mechanism is to preventing autoimmunity.
keypoints: ⭐ AIRE gene in thymic medullary epithelial cells drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens for negative selection
About 90% of all developing T cells are eliminated during thymic selection (positive + negative)
Failure of negative selection allows autoreactive T cells into the periphery, contributing to autoimmune disease
Mature dendritic cells in the thymic medulla also participate in presenting self-antigen for negative selection

questions.stem: A blood sample from an individual with systemic lupus erythematosus was studied, and many T cells were discovered to express receptors specific for autologous antigens. Failure of which process in the thymus leads to the large number of autoreactive T cells in the patient's blood?
questions.explanation: Autoreactive T cells circulating in the blood indicate a failure of negative selection, the thymic process responsible for deleting T cells with TCRs that bind self-antigen with high affinity. Affinity maturation is a peripheral B-cell process occurring in germinal centers, not a thymic T-cell selection event. Receptor editing is a B-cell (not T-cell) process occurring in the bone marrow, and hematopoiesis/antigen processing are unrelated to self-tolerance mechanisms.
keypoints: ⭐ Failure of negative selection allows self-reactive T cells to escape into the periphery, predisposing to autoimmunity like SLE
Receptor editing is the analogous B-cell tolerance mechanism, occurring in the bone marrow rather than thymus
Affinity maturation is a peripheral (germinal center) process for improving antibody affinity, unrelated to central tolerance
AIRE gene mutations (as in autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1) cause defective negative selection

questions.stem: Which cytokine is essential for T-cell proliferation and is also necessary for the production of CD25-positive regulatory T cells?
questions.explanation: IL-2 is the principal T-cell growth factor, driving clonal proliferation of activated T cells, and it is also required for the generation and maintenance of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells. IL-3 is a differentiation factor for plasmacytoid dendritic cells, IL-4 and IL-5 direct Th2 differentiation and eosinophil growth respectively, and IL-6 is a proinflammatory cytokine that (with TGF-β) promotes Th17 differentiation while also suppressing regulatory T cell activity.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-2 drives T-cell clonal expansion and is essential for CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cell generation/maintenance
IL-2 receptor targeting (e.g., basiliximab) is used clinically as immunosuppression in transplantation
CD25 is the alpha chain of the IL-2 receptor, explaining why IL-2 is needed for Treg development
IL-6 + TGF-β drives a distinct lineage (Th17) important in autoimmune inflammation, and IL-6 antagonizes Treg activity

questions.stem: T helper cells interacting with antigen-presenting dendritic cells require signals generated by the molecular interactions of the T-cell receptor with the MHC–peptide complex. Additionally, costimulation is required to amplify the initial TCR signals provided through the T cell CD28 molecule interaction with which one of the following dendritic cell molecule(s)?
questions.explanation: CD28 on T cells provides the essential costimulatory signal by binding B7 molecules (CD80/CD86) expressed on activated antigen-presenting cells. CD4 and CD8 stabilize the MHC–TCR interaction rather than providing costimulation. CD45 is a hematopoietic cell surface marker involved in signaling but not costimulation, and CD152 (CTLA-4) also binds B7 but transmits an inhibitory rather than stimulatory signal.
keypoints: ⭐ CD28-B7 (CD80/86) interaction provides the essential 'second signal' for full T-cell activation
Without costimulation, TCR signaling alone leads to anergy rather than activation
CTLA-4 (CD152) competes with CD28 for B7 binding with higher affinity, delivering an inhibitory signal — the basis for CTLA-4-Ig (abatacept) immunosuppressive therapy
CD4/CD8 are coreceptors stabilizing MHC-TCR engagement, distinct from the costimulatory CD28-B7 axis

questions.stem: T cells stimulated by peptide–MHC complexes, displayed on antigen presenting cells, in the absence of costimulation undergo which one of the following processes?
questions.explanation: TCR engagement with peptide-MHC in the absence of the required CD28-B7 costimulatory signal results in anergy — a state of long-term functional unresponsiveness in which the T cell cannot proliferate upon subsequent re-exposure to the same antigen, even with adequate costimulation later. Activation, differentiation, and proliferation all require both signals (TCR + costimulation) together. Apoptosis, by contrast, is typically triggered through distinct death-receptor pathways such as Fas-FasL or TNF-TNFR.
keypoints: ⭐ TCR signal alone (without costimulation) = anergy, a peripheral tolerance mechanism
Anergic T cells can still produce some cytokines but cannot proliferate upon antigen re-exposure
This two-signal requirement (TCR + costimulation) is a safeguard against inappropriate T-cell activation by self-antigen
Apoptosis of T cells is mediated by distinct pathways (Fas-FasL, TNF-TNFR), not simply absent costimulation

questions.stem: Downregulation of T-cell activation is achieved by the binding of which molecule on the T cell with CD80/86 on the dendritic cell?
questions.explanation: CD152 (CTLA-4) binds CD80/86 (B7) with higher affinity than CD28 does, but transmits an inhibitory rather than stimulatory signal, thereby downregulating T-cell activation as a form of peripheral immune checkpoint control. CD28 binds the same ligands but delivers a stimulatory costimulatory signal instead. CD4, CD8, and CD45 are not B7 ligands and do not mediate this specific inhibitory interaction.
keypoints: ⭐ CTLA-4 (CD152) and CD28 both bind B7 (CD80/86), but CTLA-4 delivers an inhibitory signal with higher binding affinity
CTLA-4 blockade (ipilimumab) is used in cancer immunotherapy to remove this inhibitory brake and enhance antitumor T-cell responses
This CD28/CTLA-4 competitive system exemplifies an immune checkpoint controlling the balance between activation and tolerance
Abatacept, a CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein, is used therapeutically to suppress T-cell activation in autoimmune disease

questions.stem: Dendritic cells, macrophages, and what other cell types are considered "professional antigen presenting cells," capable of antigen presentation to T helper cells?
questions.explanation: Professional antigen-presenting cells are defined by expression of both MHC class I and class II molecules along with the machinery to process exogenous antigen; B cells meet these criteria along with dendritic cells and macrophages. Basophils, eosinophils, mast cells, and neutrophils lack MHC class II expression and the associated exogenous antigen processing machinery, so they cannot present antigen to CD4+ T helper cells.
keypoints: ⭐ The three professional APCs are dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells — all express MHC class II
B cells uniquely present antigen via their B-cell receptor (surface immunoglobulin), which also serves as their specific antigen receptor
Dendritic cells are the most potent professional APCs for priming naive T cells
Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, mast cells) lack MHC class II and cannot serve as professional APCs

questions.stem: Antigens from which one of the following microbes would be presented on MHC class I molecules by macrophages?
questions.explanation: MHC class I presents endogenous antigens synthesized within the cytoplasm of the presenting cell itself. Influenza virus is an obligate intracellular pathogen that replicates within macrophages and other infected cells, generating endogenous viral peptides loaded onto MHC class I. The other pathogens listed (a helminth, a fungus, and two extracellular bacteria) do not invade the cytoplasm of macrophages and thus generate only exogenous antigens presented via MHC class II — except when cross-presented by dendritic cells specifically, which macrophages cannot do.
keypoints: ⭐ MHC class I presents endogenous (cytoplasmic) antigens — only intracellular pathogens like viruses qualify via this route in macrophages
Cross-presentation, the ability to load exogenous antigen onto MHC class I, is a unique property of dendritic cells, not macrophages
MHC class I is expressed on essentially all nucleated cells, allowing CD8+ CTLs to survey for intracellular infection anywhere in the body
Extracellular bacteria, fungi, and helminths are generally restricted to the exogenous/MHC class II presentation pathway

questions.stem: Activation of macrophages is best achieved by which cytokine?
questions.explanation: IFN-γ, produced primarily by Th1 cells (themselves differentiated under the influence of macrophage-derived IL-12), is the principal activator of macrophages, enhancing their phagocytic and microbicidal capacity — this forms a positive feedback loop central to granuloma formation and control of intracellular pathogens like Mycobacterium tuberculosis. GM-CSF differentiates granulocytes from stem cells rather than activating mature macrophages, IL-1 promotes inflammation once macrophages are already activated, MCP is a chemotactic (not activating) factor, and TGF-β generally suppresses T-cell/macrophage activity.
keypoints: ⭐ IFN-γ from Th1 cells is the key macrophage-activating cytokine, forming a Th1-macrophage feedback loop (macrophage IL-12 → Th1 IFN-γ)
This IFN-γ-macrophage loop is central to granuloma formation in tuberculosis
TGF-β is generally immunosuppressive, opposing macrophage/T-cell activation
IFN-γ receptor or IL-12 pathway defects predispose to disseminated mycobacterial infections

questions.stem: The intracellular signal initiated by antigen binding to the T-cell receptor is generated by which set of molecules expressed on the T cell membrane?
questions.explanation: CD3 is a complex of invariant signaling chains associated with the TCR that transduces the intracellular signal following antigen-MHC recognition, since the TCR itself has only a short cytoplasmic tail and lacks intrinsic signaling capacity. CD4 stabilizes TCR-MHC class II interactions rather than directly signaling, CD28 provides the separate costimulatory signal, CD45 is a phosphatase marking activation status, and CD152 (CTLA-4) delivers an inhibitory signal — none of these transduce the primary TCR recognition signal.
keypoints: ⭐ CD3 complex transduces the primary TCR signal — the TCR itself cannot signal alone due to its short cytoplasmic tail
CD3 is used clinically as a T-cell marker (anti-CD3 antibodies like OKT3/muromonab were early immunosuppressants)
CD4/CD8 are coreceptors that stabilize MHC-TCR binding but are distinct from the CD3 signaling complex
ITAMs (immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs) within CD3 chains recruit downstream kinases to propagate the signal

questions.stem: The interaction of which molecule on the membrane of cells with its ligand signals apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Fas (CD95) binding to its ligand FasL triggers activation of the caspase cascade, initiating apoptosis in the Fas-expressing cell. B7-CD28 interactions promote T-cell activation, CD40-CD40L drives B-cell activation and dendritic cell maturation, CTLA-4-B7 delivers inhibitory (not apoptotic) signaling, and Fc receptors mediate opsonization or ADCC — none of these directly trigger caspase-mediated apoptosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Fas (CD95)–FasL interaction is the classic death-receptor pathway triggering caspase-mediated apoptosis
Cytotoxic T cells and NK cells use both Fas-FasL and perforin/granzyme pathways to kill target cells
Fas-FasL apoptosis is important for eliminating activated T cells at the end of an immune response (activation-induced cell death)
Mutations in Fas or FasL cause autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) due to failure to eliminate autoreactive lymphocytes

questions.stem: Which one of the following cells is the major source of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1, and interleukin-12?
questions.explanation: Activated macrophages are the major producers of TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-12, cytokines that together promote inflammation and drive differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells toward the Th1 lineage. B cells can produce IL-1 but not TNF-α or IL-12; mast cells can produce TNF-α and IL-1 but not IL-12; Th1 cells produce TNF-α and IL-1 but rely on macrophage-derived IL-12 rather than producing it themselves in significant amounts; Th2 cells produce only IL-1 of these three.
keypoints: ⭐ Macrophages are the unique producer of all three: TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-12
Macrophage-derived IL-12 is the key driver of Th1 differentiation from naive CD4+ T cells
TNF-α and IL-1 are also central mediators of fever and the acute phase response
This macrophage cytokine triad initiates and sustains the cell-mediated (Th1) arm of adaptive immunity

questions.stem: Which cells are the source of interleukin-4, -5, -10, and -13?
questions.explanation: Th2 cells are the source of IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13, cytokines that collectively promote IgE class switching, eosinophil differentiation, and downregulation of Th1 responses — the classic Th2 cytokine profile associated with allergic and antiparasitic responses. B cells, macrophages, and mast cells can each produce some but not all of this specific cytokine set, and Th1 cells do not produce any of them since these cytokines actively suppress Th1 differentiation.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13 = the classic Th2 cytokine signature, driving IgE production, eosinophilia, and allergic/antiparasitic responses
IL-4 drives isotype switching to IgE; IL-5 promotes eosinophil growth and activation
Th1 and Th2 cytokines are mutually antagonistic (cross-regulation), maintaining polarized immune responses
NKT cells can also produce this Th2-type cytokine set upon activation

questions.stem: Which cells utilize reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes to kill pathogens?
questions.explanation: Macrophages (along with neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells) kill pathogens using reactive oxygen and nitrogen species along with lysosomal enzymes released during phagocytosis, a hallmark of the respiratory burst mechanism. Cytotoxic T cells and NK/NKT cells instead kill primarily through Fas-FasL interactions or granzyme/perforin release, a distinct mechanism targeting specific host cells rather than engulfed pathogens directly. Th1 cells can produce TNF-α and IFN-γ that contribute to cell death but do not themselves generate reactive species or lysosomal killing.
keypoints: ⭐ Macrophages (and granulocytes) kill via phagocytosis coupled with reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes (respiratory burst)
Contrast with cytotoxic T cells/NK cells, which kill target cells via Fas-FasL or perforin/granzyme, not phagocytic killing
Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase, impairing this reactive oxygen species-based killing
Nitric oxide synthase in activated macrophages generates reactive nitrogen species as part of this microbicidal arsenal

questions.stem: If a person had a genetic defect affecting perforin production, which cells and immune function would be affected?
choices: Cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells/cell killing
Mast cells/fusion of granules to cell membrane
questions.explanation: Perforin is produced exclusively by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, where it forms pores in target cell membranes allowing granzymes to enter the cytoplasm and initiate apoptosis. A perforin deficiency therefore selectively impairs the cell-killing function of these two lymphocyte populations, while leaving dendritic cell antigen presentation, granulocyte granule function, and macrophage/neutrophil phagocytosis intact, since these processes do not rely on perforin.
keypoints: ⭐ Perforin/granzyme killing is unique to cytotoxic T cells and NK cells among immune effector cells
Perforin deficiency causes familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome
Perforin forms membrane pores permitting granzyme entry, which then triggers caspase-mediated apoptosis in the target cell
This mechanism is distinct from Fas-FasL apoptosis, though both are used by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells

questions.stem: Which immune system cell is primarily responsible for the formation of granuloma in the lungs of tuberculosis patients?
questions.explanation: Granulomas form primarily through the coordinated action of macrophages and Th1 cells, working in a reinforcing feedback loop: macrophage-derived IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation, and Th1-derived IFN-γ activates macrophages to contain intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Cytotoxic T cells, dendritic cells, and NK cells are present in relatively small numbers within granulomas and are not the primary drivers, and eosinophils do not participate meaningfully in the antimycobacterial granulomatous response.
keypoints: ⭐ Granuloma formation is driven by the Th1-macrophage feedback loop: macrophage IL-12 → Th1 IFN-γ → macrophage activation
Granulomas represent a form of contained chronic inflammation that can 'wall off' but not always eliminate M. tuberculosis
Caseating necrosis at the center of TB granulomas reflects macrophage/tissue death within this immune response
TNF-α (also from Th1/macrophages) is critical for granuloma maintenance — TNF inhibitor drugs (e.g., infliximab) can reactivate latent TB

questions.stem: Which one of the following cytokines plays the most important role in protection against intracellular growth (reactivation) of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: IFN-γ is the key cytokine protecting against reactivation of latent M. tuberculosis, since it activates macrophages to enhance their intracellular killing capacity via the Th1-macrophage feedback loop. IL-2 promotes early Th1 proliferation but is not the primary effector against chronic mycobacterial infection; IL-5 and IL-10 are Th2-associated and do not participate in mycobacterial containment; TNF-α is produced by Th1 cells and synergizes with IFN-γ, but IFN-γ remains the dominant, most essential cytokine for this protection.
keypoints: ⭐ IFN-γ is the principal cytokine for macrophage activation and containment of M. tuberculosis
IFN-γ pathway defects (e.g., IFN-γ receptor deficiency, IL-12 receptor deficiency) predispose to disseminated mycobacterial disease
TNF-α acts synergistically with IFN-γ but is secondary in importance for granuloma-mediated containment
This is the immunologic basis for anti-TNF biologics increasing risk of TB reactivation

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child has atopic dermatitis due to severe allergies to dust, animal dander, and many kinds of pollens. Mediators released from which cell type are responsible for the clinical manifestations immediately following exposure to these substances?
questions.explanation: Allergen-specific IgE, generated during sensitization, binds to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells. Upon re-exposure to allergen, cross-linking of this bound IgE triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing histamine and other vasoactive mediators that produce the immediate clinical manifestations of allergy (itching, swelling, erythema). B cells produce the initial IgE but do not release these mediators themselves; Th2 cells promote IgE class switching but are not the immediate effector cells, and Th1 cells/macrophages are associated with delayed-type (not immediate) hypersensitivity.
keypoints: ⭐ Mast cell degranulation (triggered by IgE cross-linking) is responsible for immediate-phase allergic symptoms
This is a classic type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction — sensitization (IgE production) then occurs on first exposure, symptoms on re-exposure
Th2 cells drive the IgE class switch in B cells via IL-4, setting up the sensitization phase
Late-phase allergic reactions (hours later) involve eosinophil and additional inflammatory cell recruitment

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with severe allergy to yellow jackets was stung multiple times at a soccer game. Within minutes she developed respiratory distress and became unconscious. Which mediator is primarily responsible for this reaction?
questions.explanation: This describes anaphylaxis, a severe systemic type I hypersensitivity reaction triggered by IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation upon venom re-exposure. Histamine, released from mast cell granules, causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction, producing the rapid respiratory distress and hypotension/loss of consciousness seen here. Complement, IgG, and TNF play secondary or unrelated roles, and norepinephrine is actually the treatment (epinephrine) for anaphylaxis rather than a causative mediator.
keypoints: ⭐ Anaphylaxis = systemic IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation; histamine is the primary mediator of the acute symptoms
Epinephrine (not norepinephrine) is the first-line emergency treatment, counteracting histamine's vascular and bronchial effects
Repeated stings in a previously sensitized individual place them at high risk for anaphylaxis on re-exposure
Other mast cell mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins) contribute to the sustained/late-phase symptoms

questions.stem: A person develops a viral infection and both T and B cells become activated to fight the infection. In which way is antigen recognition by B cells different from antigen recognition by T cells?
choices: B cells home to the paracortex of lymph nodes where they recognize the antigens trapped by helper T cells
B cells recognize the antigens that have been processed and presented by follicular dendritic cells
B cells undergo receptor editing to change receptors that fail to bind to an antigen
B cells utilize membrane immunoglobulin molecules to bind to antigen in its natural state
The antigen receptors on a single B cell have a broad specificity, and are able to recognize several chemically unrelated antigens
questions.explanation: Unlike T cells, which can only recognize antigen after it has been processed and presented as peptide fragments on MHC molecules, B cells recognize antigen directly in its native, unprocessed conformation via membrane-bound immunoglobulin (the B-cell receptor). After this initial encounter, B cells traffic to the paracortex to interact with helper T cells and receive CD40L/cytokine signals, eventually forming germinal centers where antigen is presented by follicular dendritic cells to select high-affinity clones — but the initial recognition event itself is MHC-independent and direct.
keypoints: ⭐ B cells recognize native, unprocessed antigen directly via surface immunoglobulin — no MHC processing required, unlike T cells
Germinal center selection by follicular dendritic cells and T-cell help occurs after this initial direct recognition step
Receptor editing occurs earlier, during B-cell development in the bone marrow, not during a peripheral immune response
Each B-cell receptor has a single, defined specificity (like T-cell receptors), not broad multi-antigen recognition

questions.stem: In the primary infection above, B cells activated in a primary infection secrete which class of antibody first?
questions.explanation: IgM is the first antibody isotype produced during a primary immune response, reflecting the fact that it is also the default isotype of the naive B-cell receptor before any class switching occurs. IgG, IgA, and IgE all require isotype switching (driven by specific T-cell-derived cytokine and CD40L signals) and therefore appear later in the response. IgD has an unclear function and circulates at low levels alongside IgM on naive B cells but is not a secreted effector antibody in this context.
keypoints: ⭐ IgM is always the first antibody isotype secreted in a primary immune response, prior to any class switching
Isotype switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE requires CD40L-CD40 interaction plus specific cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ for IgG, IL-4 for IgE)
Detecting pathogen-specific IgM is used clinically to diagnose acute/recent infection
Memory responses (secondary exposure) predominantly and rapidly produce IgG due to prior class switching

questions.stem: The viral infection above began in the respiratory tract. Which antibody class would best protect respiratory epithelial cells from viral infection?
questions.explanation: IgA is the dominant antibody isotype secreted at mucosal surfaces, including the respiratory epithelium, where it is transported across epithelial cells via the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor and released as secretory IgA. This positions IgA to directly neutralize viruses at the mucosal surface before they can invade epithelial cells, making it the most relevant protective antibody at this initial site of infection. The other isotypes are found predominantly in blood or serve other functions rather than mucosal defense.
keypoints: ⭐ Secretory IgA is the primary mucosal antibody, protecting respiratory and GI epithelial surfaces from pathogen entry
Secretory IgA is a dimer linked by the J chain and contains a secretory piece that protects it from proteolytic degradation in mucosal secretions
IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and predisposes to recurrent mucosal (respiratory/GI) infections
Breast milk IgA provides passive mucosal immunity to breastfeeding infants

questions.stem: The virus above spreads from the respiratory tract and causes viremia. Which antibody class would be most important in fighting the virus as it spreads through the body?
questions.explanation: IgG is the predominant antibody isotype in the bloodstream and is the most important isotype for controlling viremia (virus circulating in the blood), functioning through complement activation, opsonization, and antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity. While IgM is also present in blood at meaningful levels, IgG is the more significant contributor to systemic antiviral defense. IgA is concentrated in mucosal secretions rather than blood, IgD's function is largely unknown, and IgE does not participate in antiviral defense.
keypoints: ⭐ IgG is the dominant blood-borne antibody isotype, key for controlling viremia via complement activation, opsonization, and ADCC
IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus/newborn
IgG has the longest half-life of the antibody isotypes, contributing to long-term humoral immunity
This contrasts with IgA's role at mucosal surfaces, illustrating isotype-specific anatomic specialization

questions.stem: In order for class switching from IgM to IgG to occur, B cells must receive two signals, one generated following binding to T helper cells and the other secreted by helper T cells. What are these two T helper cell-derived molecules?
questions.explanation: Class switching from IgM to IgG requires two T-helper-cell-derived signals: the contact-dependent interaction of CD40 ligand on the T cell with CD40 on the B cell, and the cytokine interferon-γ (secreted by Th1 cells), which specifically directs switching to IgG. In contrast, IL-4/IL-13 direct switching to IgE, while IL-2 and IL-7 do not influence isotype switching directly. CTLA-4, B7, and CD20 are not T-helper-derived signals relevant to this specific switching event.
keypoints: ⭐ IgM→IgG switching requires CD40L-CD40 contact plus IFN-γ (from Th1 cells) as the specific cytokine signal
IgM→IgE switching instead requires IL-4/IL-13 (Th2-derived cytokines) alongside the same CD40L-CD40 contact signal
CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome, in which B cells cannot switch isotypes and remain stuck producing IgM
This illustrates how cytokine milieu (Th1 vs Th2) directs the specific antibody isotype outcome of class switching

questions.stem: What structural feature is uniquely found on IgA in breast milk and not found on serum IgM?
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA found in breast milk and other mucosal secretions has a unique secretory piece (secretory component), derived from the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor during transcytosis across epithelial cells, which protects the antibody from proteolytic degradation. While both IgA (as a dimer) and IgM (as a pentamer) contain a J chain that links their subunits, only IgA in secretions acquires the additional secretory piece. Fab, hinge region, and Fc receptors are general antibody/cell-surface structural features not unique to secretory IgA.
keypoints: ⭐ Secretory piece is unique to secretory IgA, gained during transcytosis across mucosal epithelium via the polymeric Ig receptor
The secretory piece protects IgA from enzymatic degradation in harsh mucosal environments (gut, respiratory tract)
Both IgA (dimer) and IgM (pentamer) share the J chain, which links their monomeric subunits — this is not unique to IgA
This structural adaptation reflects IgA's specialized role in mucosal/external secretions rather than serum

questions.stem: Macrophages recognize microorganisms through the interaction of microbial substances with what type of receptors on macrophages?
questions.explanation: Macrophages recognize microbes via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs, such as Toll-like receptors) that bind conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) present on broad classes of microorganisms, enabling rapid innate detection without prior antigen exposure. Antigen receptors and membrane immunoglobulin are adaptive immune receptors specific to T and B cells respectively, generated by gene rearrangement rather than recognizing conserved microbial patterns. Complement and Fc receptors instead recognize host opsonins (C3b/C4b or antibody) already bound to the pathogen, not the microbe directly.
keypoints: ⭐ Pattern recognition receptors (e.g., TLRs) on macrophages detect conserved PAMPs, enabling immediate innate recognition of pathogens
This is distinct from adaptive antigen receptors (TCR/BCR), which are generated by random gene rearrangement and are pathogen-specific
Complement receptors and Fc receptors instead recognize opsonized (antibody- or complement-coated) pathogens, an indirect recognition mechanism
PRR engagement triggers proinflammatory cytokine production and phagocytosis, bridging innate to adaptive immunity

questions.stem: Antigen receptors on T and B cells share which similar feature?
choices: Affinity maturation occurs following antigen recognition for both receptor types
Interaction with MHC molecules is required for antigen recognition by both receptor types
The constant regions of both receptor types are identical
The specificity of both receptor types is determined following exposure of mature cells to antigen
The variable portions of both receptor types are generated by random recombination of genes
questions.explanation: Both TCR and BCR variable region diversity is generated through random recombination of gene segments (V(D)J recombination) during lymphocyte development in the bone marrow (B cells) or thymus (T cells), occurring before antigen exposure and independent of it. This contrasts with affinity maturation, which is a B-cell-specific process occurring in germinal centers after antigen encounter. MHC interaction is required only for T cells (not B cells), and the constant regions differ substantially between the two receptor types, reflecting their distinct downstream functions.
keypoints: ⭐ V(D)J recombination generates receptor diversity for both TCR and BCR, occurring during development, before antigen exposure
Specificity is fixed before antigen exposure — antigen exposure selects/expands cells with matching receptors, it does not create specificity
Affinity maturation (somatic hypermutation in germinal centers) is unique to B cells, not shared with T cells
MHC restriction (need for antigen presented on MHC) applies only to T cells; B cells recognize native antigen directly

questions.stem: Thymocytes interacting with self-peptides undergo negative selection. The self-peptides in this reaction act as:
questions.explanation: Self-peptides presented by thymic antigen-presenting cells during negative selection function as tolerogens — molecules that specifically promote immune tolerance (deletion of self-reactive clones) rather than eliciting an immune response. Allergens elicit IgE-mediated responses, haptens require carrier proteins to become immunogenic, and immunogens/antigens are broader terms encompassing any structure capable of provoking immunity — none of which specifically capture the tolerance-inducing role these self-peptides play in central selection.
keypoints: ⭐ Tolerogens are self-antigens presented specifically to induce tolerance (clonal deletion) rather than an immune response
This terminology distinguishes central tolerance mechanisms from terms describing foreign antigen-driven immune activation
AIRE-dependent expression of tissue-specific self-antigens in the thymic medulla provides the tolerogen repertoire for negative selection
Peripheral tolerance mechanisms (e.g., Tregs, anergy) provide backup for self-antigens not represented during thymic (central) tolerance

questions.stem: Persons with helminth infections mount immunologic responses that involve IgE and eosinophils. Which two cytokines are most important for these responses to occur?
choices: IL-10 and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β)
questions.explanation: IL-4 drives B-cell isotype switching to IgE, while IL-5 promotes eosinophil differentiation, activation, and chemotaxis — together these two Th2-derived cytokines orchestrate the IgE/eosinophil-mediated antihelminth response. IL-1/TNF promote general inflammation, IL-10/TGF-β are immunosuppressive, IL-12/IFN-γ drive the opposing Th1 pathway (relevant to intracellular pathogens), and type I interferons are antiviral rather than antihelminthic cytokines.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-4 drives IgE class switching; IL-5 drives eosinophil production/activation — together, the core antihelminth cytokine pair
IgE bound to eosinophil Fc receptors mediates antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity (ADCC) against helminths
This Th2-driven response is distinct from the Th1/IFN-γ-driven response used against intracellular pathogens
Elevated eosinophil counts (eosinophilia) and elevated IgE are classic laboratory clues to helminth infection

questions.stem: A person developed an extracellular bacterial infection, and IgM was made in response. What is the most important protective function of IgM in this infection?
questions.explanation: IgM is the most efficient antibody isotype at activating the classical complement pathway due to its pentameric structure providing multiple binding sites for C1q. Complement activation generates the opsonin C3b (enhancing phagocytosis) and the chemoattractant C5a (recruiting neutrophils), making this the most important protective mechanism of IgM against extracellular bacteria. IgM itself is not an opsonin (unlike IgG), cannot directly lyse bacteria without complement assistance, does not mediate ADCC, and while it can neutralize toxins, this is not its primary protective role in this context.
keypoints: ⭐ IgM's pentameric structure makes it highly efficient at classical complement pathway activation via C1q binding
Complement activation generates C3b (opsonization) and C5a (neutrophil chemotaxis) — the key downstream protective effects
Unlike IgG, IgM itself does not function as a direct opsonin (does not bind Fc receptors on phagocytes efficiently)
No antibody directly lyses bacteria without complement — bacterial killing requires the complement membrane attack complex

questions.stem: Neutrophils are attracted to the sites of extracellular bacterial infections by which two important chemotactic substances?
choices: Leukotriene B4 and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)
questions.explanation: Complement C5a and IL-8 (CXCL-8) are the two most important chemotactic factors recruiting neutrophils to sites of extracellular bacterial infection. Bacterial mannose and LPS serve as ligands for pattern recognition receptors rather than chemoattractants; histamine is a vasoactive mediator and C3b functions as an opsonin rather than chemoattractant; IL-7 and IL-16 support cell survival/activation but not neutrophil chemotaxis specifically; and while leukotriene B4 does have chemotactic properties, G-CSF is primarily a growth factor rather than a chemoattractant.
keypoints: ⭐ C5a (complement) and IL-8/CXCL-8 (chemokine) are the principal neutrophil chemoattractants at bacterial infection sites
C5a is generated by complement activation and also has direct proinflammatory/anaphylatoxin effects
IL-8 is a CXC chemokine produced by macrophages and epithelial cells in response to infection
Neutrophil recruitment follows a multistep adhesion cascade (rolling, adhesion, transmigration) guided by these chemotactic gradients

questions.stem: Plasma cells secreting IgA are especially abundant in which body site?
choices: Germinal centers of cervical lymph nodes
questions.explanation: The lamina propria underlying mucosal epithelium (gut, respiratory tract, genitourinary tract) contains the highest concentration of IgA-secreting plasma cells, reflecting IgA's specialized role in mucosal immunity. While IgA-producing cells can also be found in the bone marrow, lymph node germinal centers, and splenic white pulp, none of these sites approach the density found in the mucosal lamina propria, where local IgA production and secretion is essential for protecting vulnerable epithelial surfaces.
keypoints: ⭐ The lamina propria of mucosal tissue (gut, respiratory tract) is the primary site of IgA-secreting plasma cell residence
This anatomic localization supports IgA's role as the dominant mucosal antibody, secreted directly at epithelial surfaces
Long-lived plasma cells producing other isotypes (e.g., IgG) preferentially home to the bone marrow instead
Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT, including Peyer patches) is a major site initiating IgA-committed B-cell responses

questions.stem: Which immune system cells recognize body cells with reduced expression of MHC class I molecules?
