questions.explanation: Natural killer cells specifically recognize and kill host cells with reduced or absent MHC class I expression, a strategy termed 'missing self' recognition that detects a common viral immune-evasion tactic (downregulation of MHC I to escape cytotoxic T cell detection). Cytotoxic T cells, by contrast, require MHC class I presentation of specific antigenic peptides to recognize and kill infected cells — they do not respond to loss of MHC I itself. Dendritic cells, macrophages, and neutrophils are phagocytic/antigen-presenting cells and do not use MHC class I loss as a killing trigger.
keypoints: ⭐ NK cells use 'missing self' recognition — they kill cells with reduced/absent MHC class I, complementing CTLs which need MHC I present
This creates a dilemma for viruses: downregulating MHC I evades CTLs but exposes cells to NK cell killing
NK cell activity is governed by a balance of inhibitory (MHC I-sensing) and activating receptor signals
Tumor cells that downregulate MHC I to escape CTL recognition remain vulnerable to NK cell surveillance

questions.stem: Activation of the complement system directly results in which one of the following outcomes?
choices: Expression of Toll-like receptors on phagocyte cell surface
Interaction of Fc receptors with antibodies bound to antigens on the pathogen cell surface
questions.explanation: Complement activation produces three major direct outcomes: promotion of inflammation via anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) recruiting phagocytes, opsonization via C3b/C4b binding pathogens to enhance phagocytosis through complement receptors, and direct target cell killing via the membrane attack complex (C5b-C9). Toll-like receptor expression is constitutive (though inducible by other stimuli), neutralization is an antibody function unrelated to complement, T-cell proliferation is not a direct complement effect, and Fc receptor-antibody interactions represent a separate opsonization pathway not directly caused by complement activation.
keypoints: ⭐ Complement activation has three direct effects: inflammation (C3a/C5a), opsonization (C3b/C4b → enhanced phagocytosis), and lysis (MAC/C5b-C9)
C3b and C4b are the key opsonins recognized by complement receptors on phagocytes, driving enhanced phagocytosis
Neutralization and Fc receptor-mediated opsonization are antibody-driven processes that operate independently of complement
The three complement pathways (classical, alternative, lectin) all converge on C3 cleavage to produce these effects

questions.stem: Which one of the following leukocytes is considered a "granulocyte"?
questions.explanation: Granulocytes are leukocytes containing cytoplasmic granules filled with inflammatory enzymes and mediators, released upon activation; neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils comprise this category. Macrophages and dendritic cells are monocytic lineage cells lacking distinct cytoplasmic granules. NK cells and NKT cells do contain granules (perforin/granzyme) but are classified as large granular lymphocytes rather than true granulocytes, a distinct cell lineage.
keypoints: ⭐ True granulocytes = neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — distinguished by prominent cytoplasmic granules and multilobed nuclei
NK/NKT cells contain granules (perforin, granzyme) but are classified separately as 'large granular lymphocytes,' not granulocytes
Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocyte and the primary responder to acute bacterial infection
Monocyte-lineage cells (macrophages, dendritic cells) lack the distinct granule morphology defining granulocytes

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents with anorexia and some abdominal pain. Fecal smears reveal the presence of Taenia eggs, products of a parasitic tapeworm infection. Which one of the following cells would be most effective in defense against this parasite?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils express high-affinity Fc receptors for IgE (FcεRI), allowing them to bind IgE-coated parasitic organisms and mediate antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity, releasing cytotoxic granule contents (major basic protein and others) directly onto the parasite surface. This makes eosinophils the most effective cellular defense against multicellular parasites such as tapeworms, which are too large to be phagocytosed by neutrophils or monocytes. Platelets and erythrocytes are not immune effector cells in this context.
keypoints: ⭐ Eosinophils are the key effector cells against helminths, using IgE-mediated ADCC via FcεRI to kill parasites too large to phagocytose
Major basic protein, released from eosinophil granules, is directly toxic to helminth parasites
This is the same IgE/eosinophil axis that also underlies allergic disease pathophysiology (an evolutionary 'misfiring')
Peripheral eosinophilia is a classic laboratory clue pointing toward helminth (parasitic) infection

questions.stem: Antigen presenting cells (APCs) are required for T-cell recognition of specific antigen and activation. APCs accomplish this task by presenting antigen in the context of which of the following molecules?
questions.explanation: Antigen presenting cells display processed peptide antigens bound within MHC molecules (class I or II) on their surface, which is the molecular context that T-cell receptors recognize. TLRs are innate pattern recognition receptors that detect microbial components and trigger inflammatory cytokine production but do not themselves present antigen. FcR mediates opsonization/antibody binding, and KIR is an NK cell receptor family for MHC class I sensing — neither functions in antigen presentation to T cells.
keypoints: ⭐ MHC (class I or II) is the molecule that displays processed antigen for T-cell receptor recognition
All nucleated cells express MHC class I; only professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) additionally express MHC class II
TLRs trigger APC activation/maturation and cytokine production but are functionally distinct from the MHC antigen-display machinery
This MHC restriction is a defining feature of T-cell antigen recognition, contrasting with B cells recognizing native antigen directly

questions.stem: A 1-year-old female presented with symptoms of systemic autoimmunity (lupus, diabetes, and arthritis), and upon genetic analysis it was found that the patient had a mutation in the Foxp3 gene locus. Which one of the following is an explanation for the clinical symptoms observed?
choices: Patient cannot produce antigen presenting cells
Patient cannot generate regulatory CD4+CD25+ T cells
Patient is unable to produce antibodies
Patient NK cells have no inhibitory signal
questions.explanation: Foxp3 is the master transcription factor required for development and suppressive function of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), which maintain peripheral tolerance by suppressing self-reactive T cells that escaped thymic negative selection. Loss-of-function Foxp3 mutations (as in IPEX syndrome — immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked) prevent Treg generation, leading to widespread multiorgan autoimmunity. The other options describe unrelated immune defects not caused by Foxp3 mutation.
keypoints: ⭐ Foxp3 is the master transcription factor for regulatory T cell (Treg) development — its loss causes IPEX syndrome
IPEX presents in infancy with severe multiorgan autoimmunity (enteropathy, endocrinopathy, dermatitis) due to unchecked autoreactive T cells
Tregs act via poorly defined cell-contact-dependent inhibitory mechanisms to suppress self-reactive T cells in the periphery
This illustrates peripheral tolerance as a backup to central (thymic) tolerance, preventing autoimmunity from self-reactive escapees

questions.stem: Following an initial expansion of B cells in response to microbial peptides, a memory pool of B cells is generated and maintained throughout life, along with a second memory cell type. Upon rechallenge with the microbe, the patient is protected from infection. Which one of the following explanations accounts for this observation?
choices: Circulating memory B cells are actively producing antibodies in the absence of antigen
Circulating memory B cells will produce antibodies, however, only upon encounter with the microbial antigen
Long-lived plasma cells are actively producing antibodies in the absence of antigen
Long-lived plasma cells will produce antibodies, however, only upon encounter with the microbial antigen
TLR signaling to the circulating memory B cells will induce rapid production of antibodies in response to antigen encounter
questions.explanation: Long-lived plasma cells, generated from an initial B-cell response, take up residence in the bone marrow and continuously secrete antibody even in the complete absence of ongoing antigen exposure, providing durable baseline protective antibody titers. Circulating memory B cells, by contrast, do not actively secrete antibody at baseline; instead they serve as a rapidly expandable reserve, only differentiating into new antibody-secreting cells upon re-encountering antigen, providing the fast anamnestic response characteristic of secondary immunity.
keypoints: ⭐ Long-lived plasma cells reside in bone marrow and continuously secrete antibody without needing antigen re-exposure — the source of durable protective titers
Memory B cells, unlike long-lived plasma cells, are quiescent until antigen re-exposure, then rapidly differentiate for the anamnestic response
This two-tiered system (baseline antibody from plasma cells + rapid-response reserve from memory B cells) is the basis for long-term vaccine protection
Vaccine boosters work by re-stimulating memory B cells to generate additional long-lived plasma cells and higher-affinity antibody

questions.stem: Which one of the following represents the mechanism by which immune complexes (ICs) are normally cleared from the circulation?
choices: Factor I releases complement-bound ICs to bind with complement receptors found on splenic/hepatic neutrophils
Red blood cells capture ICs from blood via Fc receptors
C3b solubilizes ICs and attaches to red blood cells via complement receptors
questions.explanation: Immune complexes are normally cleared through a complement-dependent mechanism: C3b generated during complement activation binds to and helps solubilize the immune complex, then attaches to complement receptors (CR1) on red blood cells. These red cells carry the bound complexes through the circulation to the spleen and liver, where resident macrophages remove the complexes from the red cell surface for degradation, without destroying the red cells themselves. Defects in this complement-mediated clearance pathway underlie immune complex diseases like SLE, where persistent circulating immune complexes deposit in tissues and cause damage.
keypoints: ⭐ C3b binds immune complexes and attaches them to CR1 on red blood cells, which ferry the complexes to spleen/liver macrophages for removal
Red blood cells use Fc receptors is a common distractor — the actual mechanism uses complement receptors (CR1), not Fc receptors
This clearance mechanism explains why complement deficiencies predispose to immune complex-mediated diseases like SLE
Splenic and hepatic macrophages (not neutrophils) perform the final removal/degradation of the complexes from red cells

questions.stem: Which of the following is the site at which lymphocytes can leave the blood and gain entry into the lymph nodes and what lymphocyte cell surface protein mediates such access?
questions.explanation: Naive lymphocytes exit the bloodstream and enter lymph nodes through specialized high endothelial venules (HEV), where CD62L (L-selectin) on the lymphocyte surface mediates initial rolling/arrest via binding to addressins on the HEV endothelium, followed by chemokine-directed transmigration into the node cortex. Lymphoid follicles and germinal centers are destination zones within the node for B-cell activity, not entry points from blood, and PALS is a splenic (not lymph node) T-cell zone.
keypoints: ⭐ High endothelial venules (HEV) are the specialized vascular entry point for lymphocytes into lymph nodes, mediated by CD62L (L-selectin)
CD62L-mediated rolling is followed by chemokine-triggered integrin activation and firm adhesion/transmigration
PALS (periarterial lymphatic sheath) is the T-cell zone of the splenic white pulp, distinct from lymph node HEV entry
This trafficking pathway is central to immune surveillance, allowing continuous lymphocyte recirculation between blood and lymphoid tissue

questions.stem: The difference between tolerance and immunity depends upon the maturation status of the antigen presenting dendritic cells. What is the T-cell outcome of an antigen presentation event by a mature dendritic cell?
questions.explanation: Mature dendritic cells, having been activated via Toll-like receptor engagement by pathogen components, upregulate B7 costimulatory molecules; when this mature, costimulation-competent dendritic cell presents antigen via MHC-peptide complex to a T cell, the result is full T-cell activation. Immature dendritic cells lacking sufficient B7 expression instead induce anergy upon antigen presentation, since TCR engagement occurs without adequate costimulation — illustrating how DC maturation state functions as a checkpoint distinguishing tolerance from active immunity.
keypoints: ⭐ DC maturation state is the key determinant of activation vs. tolerance outcome: mature DCs (high B7) → T-cell activation; immature DCs (low B7) → anergy
Toll-like receptor engagement by pathogen components is the trigger driving dendritic cell maturation and B7 upregulation
'Ignorance' describes a distinct tolerance mechanism where antigen is sequestered from T-cell access entirely (e.g., immune-privileged sites)
This DC maturation checkpoint is a key reason why adjuvants (which activate innate signaling) are needed in vaccines to generate robust immunity
